questionText: A colleague says "I tried AI, it gave me a wrong answer, so I don't trust it." What is the most useful response?

answerOptions.text: Agree, AI is unreliable for serious work.
Calibrate trust per task type: decide when to verify.
Wait six months for the technology to improve.

explanation: Trust depends on how often the model is right for that task and what a failure costs. Writing AI off after one wrong answer skips that calibration, as does trusting it after one right one.

questionText: Which best describes L3 (Conductor)?

answerOptions.text: You use Cursor or Claude Code for autocomplete daily.
AI writes your first draft of every doc.
You direct several agents in parallel and delegate whole tasks.
You have read three books on AI.

explanation: At L3 the unit of work is a delegation: you assign, check in and redirect while agents do the spec-to-PR work. Daily autocomplete is L1 and AI-first drafts are L2.

questionText: A senior engineer hand-codes a feature overnight to "prove they still can." How does an AI-native leader respond?

answerOptions.text: Praise the craft privately, then point it at specs and evals.
Punish them for not using AI.

explanation: Public praise for solo heroics anchors the culture on hours and individual effort. The same taste applied to specs, evals and review carries a whole fleet.

questionText: What is the most important section of an agent spec?

answerOptions.text: The opening sentence and the test cases

explanation: The opening sentence sets the goal the agent optimizes for, and the test cases define what "correct" means. Long prose in the middle does little and invites drift when vague.

questionText: A teammate ships an agent change without running the eval suite. What is the right response?

answerOptions.text: Allow it; evals slow things down.
Block the change until the eval suite passes.
Add a comment to the PR but merge anyway.

explanation: Eval-driven release lets no agent change reach production without passing the suite, enforced by the system. Skipping it once is how a model upgrade or prompt tweak silently breaks a workflow.

questionText: Your fleet of three agents is producing low-quality PRs. What is the most likely cause?

answerOptions.text: The agents need to be replaced with newer models.
Bad specs, shallow context or missing eval gates.
Agents fundamentally cannot do this work.

explanation: A fleet's output traces back to its inputs. New models or micromanaging treat the symptom; a tighter spec, deeper context and a higher eval bar treat the cause.

questionText: Which test shows whether AI is a feature or the product?

answerOptions.text: Whether it uses an LLM under the hood.
Whether the product still works without the AI.
Whether it has a chat interface.

explanation: If the product still works without the AI, the AI was a bolt-on. If it does not, the reasoning system is the product's engine.

questionText: A flow has 7 steps after the user states intent. The AI-native instinct is:

answerOptions.text: Add a chat bubble for help.
Compress the 7 steps into one delegated action.

explanation: Collapse the steps after the stated intent into one delegated action. A help bubble or tooltip makes a long flow easier to tolerate, but it stays long.

questionText: Generative UI is most appropriate for:

answerOptions.text: Surfaces where user intent varies widely, such as dashboards.

explanation: Dashboards, homepages and settings serve users with very different goals, which one fixed layout cannot cover. Payment and legal flows need consistency, so they stay static.

questionText: A weekly status meeting with 8 attendees mostly reports information already in writing. The right move is:

answerOptions.text: Go async with an AI summary; keep live time for decisions.

explanation: An agent can summarize the written channel for conflicts, blockers and needed decisions. Shortening or reordering the meeting only trims the coordination cost.

questionText: A triage agent handles ~95% of tickets without human touch. Which 5% should escalate to humans?

answerOptions.text: The cases where the agent flagged uncertainty.
The ones from VIP customers only.

explanation: Flagged uncertainty signals that human judgement is needed. Escalating by sample, age or customer tier spends attention on cases the agent already handles.

questionText: A live-build interview tests:

answerOptions.text: Ability to invert a binary tree.
Spec quality, agent direction, review judgement, calibrated trust and final quality.

explanation: These are the skills AI-native work depends on. Typing speed and inverting a binary tree from memory are not.

questionText: You are designing compensation tied to output. Which metric is the WORST choice?

answerOptions.text: Number of prompts sent per week.

explanation: Prompt count rewards activity, not outcomes, and is easily gamed once pay depends on it. Cycle time, defect rate and throughput move only when the work improves.

questionText: A team requests +5 headcount. AI-native leadership response is:

answerOptions.text: Ask what they tried with agents first.

explanation: The team first shows what agents could absorb before hiring becomes the lever. Approving on budget alone or denying outright both skip that test.

questionText: Specialists are most useful in an AI-native org as:

answerOptions.text: Deep individual contributors who own execution.
Advisors and reviewers who scale through judgment.

explanation: Their judgement carries across many decisions, while hands-on execution increasingly runs through generalists with agents. Using a specialist as a bottlenecked executor wastes that.

questionText: An agent returns a confidential document the calling user should not see. The right architectural fix is:

answerOptions.text: Add a content filter on the response.
Permission-aware retrieval filtered by the calling user's identity and ACLs.
Hide the agent from senior users.

explanation: No agent identity then carries elevated access. A response filter only patches the symptom; the leak stays possible until retrieval respects permissions.

questionText: Why are nightly snapshots dangerous for agentic workflows?

answerOptions.text: The agent answers from yesterday's data but acts on today's.

explanation: A deleted record, changed price or closed ticket stays invisible until the next sync, so the agent acts confidently on stale facts. Build cost and storage are not the issue.

questionText: Security asks which AI models run on customer PII right now, and you cannot answer. What is the highest-impact fix?
explanation: A registry keeps provider, version, data classification, owner and last review date current in one place. Disabling AI or hiring a CISO only reacts to the symptom.

questionText: An agent deletes a record. To answer "who did this and why," you need:

answerOptions.text: A rough estimate based on agent name.
Agent identity, acting-for user, timestamp and authorization in the audit log.

explanation: Only a log written at the moment of the action answers who did it and why. Sentiment analysis or a retrospective produces a guess.

questionText: Your AI rollout claims a 30% productivity gain. What is the hardest question a board member can ask?

answerOptions.text: What is the baseline measurement and when was it taken?

explanation: Without a baseline measured under comparable conditions, a 30% gain is a story. Model, vendor and seat count come second.

questionText: The most reliable signal that an AI program is working:

answerOptions.text: Cycle time, defect rate and throughput improving against a measured baseline.

explanation: Outcome metrics move when the work gets better. Active users, token volume and survey sentiment can rise while nothing real improves.

questionText: A quarterly review of the AI program should look most like:

answerOptions.text: A revenue review, with the same rigor and seriousness.

explanation: It reports real numbers, why they moved, to people who ask hard questions, at a fixed cadence. A status update or demo day undersells the discipline the program needs to keep funding.
